title: Suspected bacterial meningitis at 67 on vancomycin and ceftriaxone, without ampicillin

provenance.author: Claude Code (draft for owner review), scenario requested by the owner

clinical_review.notes: Owner clinical review: cases look good.

story: A 67-year-old woman presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and new confusion. Lumbar puncture shows a neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein. Empiric vancomycin, ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours and dexamethasone are started; CSF and blood cultures are pending. Ampicillin is not ordered.

expected_findings.summary: Empiric therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in a patient over 50 lacks ampicillin: cephalosporins and vancomycin do not cover Listeria monocytogenes.

reference_answer: Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours (adjusted for renal function) to vancomycin, ceftriaxone and dexamethasone until cultures exclude Listeria. With a serious penicillin allergy, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual alternative for Listeria coverage. Narrow therapy once CSF and blood cultures and Gram stain results return.
rationale: Adults older than 50 have a higher risk of Listeria monocytogenes meningitis, which is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. IDSA and ESCMID empiric regimens for this age group add ampicillin (or amoxicillin) to vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin. The finding rests on age, the working diagnosis and the absence of an ampicillin order; no culture result is needed, so it should fire while cultures are still pending.
